forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Epsom and Ewell halts £49.6m commercial property borrowing programme due to reorganisation uncertainty
news_drafts.lead: Epsom and Ewell Council has withdrawn approval to borrow £49.6 million for commercial property acquisitions, halting an investment strategy approved in February 2026. The decision reflects uncertainty over the proposed local government reorganisation, which the council says introduces "a significant degree of uncertainty and transition risk" to capital programme management. In its quarter-one capital budget monitoring, the council also deferred discretionary projects including a £120,000 wellbeing centre refurbishment and reported that contractor inflation is having "a major impact" on its ability to source works within budget. On day-to-day spending, the council recorded a £250,000 overspend on homelessness accommodation in the first quarter, driven by increased demand following May's Renters Rights Act; it has covered this from corporate contingency. The council's section 151 officer said the housing position remains "highly sensitive to fluctuations in demand, availability of accommodation and wider housing market conditions."

news_drafts.headline: Epsom and Ewell halts capital investment following government reorganization announcement
news_drafts.lead: Epsom and Ewell council has ceased acquisitions under its Commercial Property Investment Fund following the government's 28 October announcement that Surrey's current county, district and borough councils will be replaced by two unitary authorities. The council had estimated £49.6m capital expenditure on commercial properties for 2025/26 but made no property purchases, spending £2.8m against a total capital forecast of £58.3m. Meanwhile, the council's treasury performance improved: net investment income reached £1,178,313, exceeding its mid-year forecast by £236,313 despite lower average cash balances and declining interest rates. The council's average net return on investments was 4.23%, outperforming the SONIA benchmark. The council maintained its Public Works Loan Board debt flat at £64.4m and required no temporary borrowing during the year.

findings.headline: Council expresses concern that homelessness numbers may rise further with the onset of winter
findings.detail: The paper flags that homelessness numbers are expected to remain high and may rise further, particularly in winter when demand historically increases. This suggests the current overspend may worsen in the coming months.
findings.matters: Indicates the current overspend may worsen, and the council faces an ongoing budgeting challenge through the winter period.
findings.quote: Nevertheless, there is concern that homelessness numbers will remain high and possibly rise still further, particularly with the onset of winter, which historically sees increased demand.

findings.headline: No new affordable housing was delivered in the past year, constraining the council's ability to move people on from temporary accommodation
findings.detail: The paper identifies lack of newly developed affordable housing as a root cause, noting zero units were delivered in the past year. With the private rental sector also unaffordable, this creates a structural constraint that may persist despite increased spending.
findings.matters: This identifies an underlying supply-side constraint that spending more on temporary accommodation services alone cannot solve. The problem may be structural, not operational.
findings.figures: No new affordable housing units delivered in past year
findings.quote: The review of service delivery , highlights that without access to sufficient affordable accommodation, and with much of the private rental sector remaining unaffordable, temporary accommodation (TA) usage may increase further.

findings.headline: Council is allocating £750k growth budget and £128.5k in-year funding to temporary accommodation to address a structural deficit
findings.detail: The council is allocating £750k in growth funding for 2026/27 and an additional £128.5k in-year to temporary accommodation. The paper describes this as addressing a structural deficit in the service.
findings.matters: The scale of allocation shows the council recognizes this as a major problem and is taking action to manage it, but also signals the problem is substantial and structural.
findings.quote: It is worth noting that £750k growth budget was put into the nightly paid service for 2026/27 to address some of the structural deficit in this area . Furthermore, the budget has been further increased by £128.5k in year, funded from the inflationary provision.

findings.headline: Homelessness applications have surged 86% in two years, with nightly paid accommodation numbers rising from approximately 20 to approximately 120
findings.detail: The paper shows homeless households in nightly paid accommodation rising from approximately 20 in April 2022 to approximately 120 by June 2026. Homelessness applications have risen each year, with recent years showing particularly steep increases.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether this demand-driven growth is unsustainable or cyclical, and whether the council can continue to fund it. Demand has roughly doubled in 2 years.
findings.figures: 86% rise in homelessness applications over two years; nightly paid accommodation rising from approximately 20 to approximately 120
findings.quote: The tables below show the total number of homeless households in nightly paid accommodation over the past four years and the huge rise (86%) in homelessness applications over the past two years.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation service shows £0.250m adverse variance in Q1 2026 due to elevated numbers of homeless households
findings.detail: The first-quarter forecast shows a £0.250m overspend in temporary accommodation. This is driven by higher than expected numbers of homeless households requiring nightly paid accommodation.
findings.matters: A material overspend in a demand-driven social care service that the council is legally obliged to fund, and one that continues to grow.
findings.quote: The updated forecast for  end June 2026 is a net adverse variance of £ 0.250m, due to the continued elevated numbers of households in temporary accommodation (TA).
